{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=conceptual+frameworks+for+AI+accountability+and+legal+liability+attribution+models&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Reclaiming human clinical reasoning in generative AI-enabled healthcare: a perspective on cognitive agency, skill evolution, and accountability.\", \"abstract\": \"Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) are transforming clinical decision support systems (CDSS) from traditional discrete predictions into fluent, context-aware clinical narrative generation. Although these capabilities substantially improve the efficiency of clinical workflows, they also introduce distinctive cognitive challenges: highly fluent and seemingly plausible medical narratives may reshape the way physicians construct clinical meaning and make analytic judgments. This perspective paper introduces the concept of Narrative Cognitive Substitution (NCS), proposed as a testable mid-level theoretical construct, which describes the hypothesized shift in human cognition from active hypothesis generation to passive retrospective validation when GenAI outputs pre-organize diagnostic reasoning and therapeutic pathways. We further propose a Skill Evolution Framework that characterizes the potential effects of GenAI on physician competence across five trajectories: Augmentation, Restructuring, Deskilling, Never-skilling, and Mis-skilling. In addition, we analyze the resulting Accountability Gap: although algorithmic outputs are increasingly embedded in clinical decision-making, decision influence is distributed across clinicians, institutions, developers, and deployers, yet professional accountability and final decision authority remain formally concentrated on the individual physician. To address these systemic challenges, we propose a human-centered governance framework -presented as design hypotheses requiring prospective evaluation- encompassing user interface design (embedding risk-adaptive cognitive friction), medical education (establishing targeted, protected AI-free reasoning exercises (\\\"Reasoning Cleanrooms\\\")), and institutional policies (implementing substantive human oversight and algorithmovigilance). Barbora Bruant Gulejova (on behalf of the IPPOG Collaboration) 
  
 
Abstract 
 
The International Particle Physics Outreach Group (IPPOG) has been making concerted and systematic efforts to 
present and populari se particle physics across all audiences and age groups since 1997 . T oday the scientific 
community has in IPPOG a strategic pillar in fostering long -term, sustainable support for fundamental research 
around the world. One of the main tools IPPOG has been offering to the scientific community, teachers and 
educators for almost 10 years is the Resource Database (RDB), an online platform containing a collection of high 
quality engaging education and outreach materials in particle physics and related sciences.  
 
1. Introduction 
 
Main challenges  the scientific community faces currently are the  threat to the financial support of large 
experimental endeavours and falling interest of young people to engage in studies of STEM (science, technology, 
engineering and mathematics), especially physics.  
In general physics is less popular than other natural sciences, suffering a stigma of being a science that  is very 
mathematical, abstract, and complicated. It is perceived as disconnected from r eal world. Most of the students  
who claim to love science do not mean physics, not realizing how fun physics can be.  
It is important to break these stereot ypes based on the misperception of physics in society. Physics is a pillar of 
all natural sciences. Physics is about understanding the basic laws of nature, the world we live in. It explains how 
the world around us and within us functions. This fundamental definition  of physics does not often come across 
to students from their physics school curriculum.

title: Socioeconomic driving forces of scientific research
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1806.05028v1
published: 2018-06-13T13:33:54Z
summary: Why do nations produce scientific research? This is a fundamental problem in the field of social studies of science. The paper confronts this question here by showing vital determinants of science to explain the sources of social power and wealth creation by nations. Firstly, this study suggests a new general definition of science and scientific research that synthetizes previous concepts and endeavors to extend them: Science discovers the root causes of phenomena to explain and predict them in a context of adaptation of life to new economic and social bases, whereas scientific research is a systematic process, applying methods of scientific inquiry, to solve consequential problems, to satisfy human wants, to take advantage of important opportunities and/or to cope with environmental threats. In particular, science and scientific research are driven by an organized social effort that inevitably reflect the concerns and interests of nations to achieve advances and discoveries that are spread to the rest of humankind.
